description: Accepted answers to open decisions O1-O8, carried from the accepted implementation contract into the machine-checkable conformance baseline. Each entry records the accepted answer, its location in the design, the real repository/design evidence it rests on, and the implementation stories that own delivering it. T0 encodes these; it does not choose or amend them.

decisions.question: Which agent implementation runs first, and how does it reach a model?
decisions.answer: agent-task-investigator: Node.js 22 / TypeScript, independent package with its own build and lockfile, native JSON process protocol over stdin/stdout, and host-mediated model requests. No agent SDK dependency. Packaged in modules/agent-factory/task-agents/investigator/ and invoked through the command allowlist with --embedded.
decisions.rationale: A bounded investigation over caller-supplied text/JSON evidence exercises useful progress, clarification and results without GitHub, shell tools or customer credentials. The child receives no AWS, GitHub, gateway or customer credential in its arguments or environment.
decisions.owner_notes: T4/T5 implement the investigator and its host adapter; T3 registers its model compatibility.
decisions.model_transport: Anthropic Messages request/response format over the existing platform proxy service. Not an assumed Converse endpoint.

decisions.question: How do external callers authenticate, and who owns authorization?
decisions.answer: Cognito client-credentials access tokens with exact cognito_m2m alias resolution to ADP's canonical service principal. The gateway owns authorization for both the ingress and the read/control paths.
decisions.rationale: Uses the existing identity system without duplicating its SQL directory inside the Lambda. Tenant resolution comes from trusted authentication and client registration, then the exact tenant/source/alias lookup in the canonical principal service. No fallback to sub, a body service name or a legacy EventBridge alias.
decisions.v1_access_model: service-owner-only; no public delegation, human-admin override, or IAM/SigV4 external submit adapter

decisions.question: Where do task records and authority live, and how are legacy semantics preserved?
decisions.answer: Distinct TASK* namespaces in the existing request table adp-<env>-webhook-events; protected task/run grants in the existing authority table; the gateway is the sole task writer; explicit worker IAM denies on every TASK* namespace and on protected authority records.
decisions.rationale: Cross-table DynamoDB transactions can commit metadata and authority together while legacy readers and writers remain separate. Task items omit the legacy GSI attributes so they cannot appear in legacy tenant/user/correlation/engine-command queries.
decisions.iam_boundary_note: Deny covers Put/Update/Delete, batch and transactional write paths using ForAnyValue:StringLike on DynamoDB LeadingKeys so a mixed legacy/task batch cannot bypass it. A Python helper or record discriminator alone is not the boundary. If the boundary cannot be proven against AWS, admission stays off.

decisions.question: How is accepted work protected against lost HTTP and queue acknowledgements?
decisions.answer: Transactional acceptance with an outbox, a stable FIFO dispatch ID, scheduled recovery through a task-recovery alias of the existing Lambda, and protected generation fencing.
decisions.rationale: A lost HTTP or SQS acknowledgement cannot lose accepted work or authorize a second active execution. Conditional bootstrap prevents concurrent execution even after FIFO deduplication expires; SQS's deduplication window is not the task's idempotency window.
decisions.alias_guard: Scheduled target has a source-scoped invoke permission; the public API integration cannot invoke that alias. Verify invoked alias/context before accepting a recovery event; an HTTP body naming recovery is never sufficient.

decisions.question: How does the worker obtain execution authority without inventing human or repository fields?
decisions.answer: TokenReview-bound queue acquisition and task-specific service-rooted bootstrap/grants through a typed task_service_policy adapter. Model policy and spend are enforced at the gateway.
decisions.rationale: Existing repository-rooted and human-rooted helpers cannot be called with invented fields. The typed adapter carries canonical service ID and policy reference; it does not fill human_id, repository or installation fields to satisfy the existing EventBridge grant, and service tasks do not impersonate a human control session.
decisions.policy_write_authority: Authenticated human organization administrator with the existing ORG_UPDATE permission and same-tenant canonical-principal validation, through GET/PUT /service-principals/{canonical_id}/task-policy. PUT requires expected_version. Services cannot self-grant task authority.
decisions.default_posture: Existing service principals are denied task execution until an explicit task policy exists.

decisions.question: How do the host and child exchange work, and what does consuming an input mean?
decisions.answer: Incremental NDJSON over child stdin/stdout, host-authenticated gateway reporting, persisted events and conversation turns, and separate logical-consumption and model-handoff receipts.
decisions.rationale: Durable input is an explicit extension of the remote-control contract. The testable consumption boundary is that one command is appended once to the canonical conversation and included once in its assigned logical turn. It does not claim exactly-once provider execution or proof that a model obeyed the input. The owner accepted this explicit boundary; it is not permission to weaken V3-07.
decisions.ambiguity_rule: A crash between claiming a model operation and the physical send is conservatively unknown. Never automatically resend a possibly-sent request; never mark unknown usage as zero.

decisions.question: What numeric limits bound the pilot?
decisions.answer: The fixed pilot limits recorded in implementation-design.md section 10, encoded in this contract as limits.json.
decisions.rationale: Bounded qualification before wider use. These are accepted baseline limits, not observed performance or authorization to spend. Implementations may enforce stricter existing platform policy but cannot relax these limits; raising one requires a reviewed design change before new acceptance measurements.

decisions.question: How does the capability roll out, and what may the engine deploy?
decisions.answer: Default-off pilot with four admission/read/worker/recovery flags, fully compatible shared consumers before publication, controlled coexistence, and drain-before-rollback. Deployment handoff as described in design section 11: supported engine bindings when bound, otherwise the documented operator path.
decisions.rationale: Existing schedules and an unresolved deployment manifest cannot establish readiness. The engine's packaged deployment manifest has unresolved gateway/migration entries and no complete Task API coverage, and registers no automatic rollback adapter, so merging code cannot be treated as a completed automated deployment.
rollout_order: finish or drain incompatible shared consumers
prove every shared-queue consumer compatible or excluded
rollback_order: retain read/control/recovery services and task-capable consumers until accepted tasks are drained, cancelled with evidence or durably quarantined
never purge the shared queue or replace the table
preserve the task record boundary in any IAM rollback while retained task data exists
decisions.mixed_image_rule: A mixed image rollout is not proof of same-queue safety. Keep admission off during the compatibility window.
